content:
Living with osteoarthritis pain and frailty can be hard, and it is common to feel low at times. For some people, low mood becomes depression, which can make pain feel worse, reduce sleep and energy, and make it harder to stay active. This can become a cycle.

This guide explains the signs of depression, how it links with pain and frailty, and where to get help. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

How pain, frailty and mood are linked

Ongoing pain can disturb sleep, limit activities you enjoy and reduce contact with other people. Losing independence can affect confidence. Depression in turn can lower energy and motivation, so people move less, become weaker and feel more pain. Treating mood can help with day-to-day life and coping with pain.

Signs of depression

The NHS describes depression as feeling low or hopeless most of the time for at least two weeks. Other signs include:

  • Losing interest or enjoyment in things.
  • Sleeping badly or much more than usual.
  • Changes in appetite or weight.
  • Feeling tired or lacking energy.
  • Feeling worthless or guilty.
  • Withdrawing from friends and family.

In older people, depression can sometimes show mainly as tiredness, aches or memory problems, so it can be missed.

Treatments and support

  • Talking therapies, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). In England you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies. In Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, ask your GP about local services.
  • Activity and exercise, which NICE recommends for both osteoarthritis and depression.
  • Medicines, such as antidepressants. Some are also used for pain. Your GP will consider your other medicines and your risk of falls.
  • Social contact, including groups, befriending and social prescribing.

Small steps that help

  • Plan one enjoyable or meaningful activity each day.
  • Get outside or near daylight if you can.
  • Keep regular sleep and meal times.
  • Tell someone you trust how you are feeling.

When to get help

  • Call 999 or go to A&E if you or someone else is in immediate danger or has seriously harmed themselves.
  • Get urgent help the same day if you are having thoughts of suicide: call NHS 111 (option 2 for mental health in England), your GP, or Samaritans on 116 123.
  • See your GP if you have felt low or lost interest in things for two weeks or more.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it normal to feel low with arthritis?

Low moods are common, but persistent low mood is not something you have to live with. It is worth talking to your GP.

Will antidepressants make me unsteady?

Some can cause drowsiness or dizziness. Your GP or pharmacist can choose and review medicines with falls in mind.

Can talking therapies help with pain?

They will not remove pain, but they can help you cope with it and improve mood and sleep.
